questions.q: The lecture was so long that I got really *___*.
questions.explain: *-ed* adjectives describe how a person feels; *-ing* adjectives describe what causes the feeling.

questions.q: Choose the natural order: She bought a *___* table.
questions.explain: Size → shape → material: *a small round wooden table*.

questions.q: Which adjective cannot normally go before a noun?
questions.explain: Adjectives starting with *a-* (*asleep, afraid, alone, alive*) usually come after a verb: *The baby is asleep*.

questions.q: This exam was *___* than the last one.
questions.explain: Two-syllable adjectives ending in *-y* take *-ier*: *easier*. Never double the comparative.

questions.q: It's the tallest building *___* the world.
questions.explain: After a superlative, use *in* with places and groups: *in the world*, *in the class*.

questions.q: This flat is *___* bigger than our old one.
questions.explain: Comparatives are strengthened with *much, far, a lot*, not *very*.

questions.q: The more you practise, *___* you get.
questions.explain: The pattern is *the + comparative …, the + comparative*: *the more…, the better*.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explain: Don't put an adverb between a verb and its object: *speaks English very well*.

questions.q: He *___* late for meetings.
questions.explain: Frequency adverbs go after the verb *be* but before other main verbs.

questions.q: Which word is an adjective, not an adverb?
questions.explain: *friendly* (like *lovely, lonely, silly*) is an adjective. Say *in a friendly way*.

questions.q: She worked *___* all day and was exhausted.
questions.explain: *hard* is the adverb meaning *with effort*; *hardly* means *almost not*.

questions.q: The film was *___* wonderful.
questions.explain: *wonderful* is an extreme adjective, so it goes with *absolutely*, not *very*.

questions.q: In British English, *The hotel was quite good* usually means…
options: it was fairly good but not great
questions.explain: With gradable adjectives, British *quite* means *fairly, but not very*.

questions.q: I'm not hungry. — I'm not hungry *___*.
questions.explain: In negative sentences we use *either*, not *too* or *also*.

questions.q: I met my best friend ten years *___*.
questions.explain: *ago* comes after the period and goes with the past simple, counting back from now.

questions.q: Have you *___* been to Japan?
questions.explain: *ever* means *at any time* and is typical in questions with the present perfect.

questions.q: It's 10 p.m. and he *___* hasn't called.
questions.explain: *still* shows a situation continuing; in negatives it goes before the auxiliary: *still hasn't*.

questions.q: We waited for hours and *___* the bus arrived.
questions.explain: *eventually* means *in the end, after a long time*. It never means *possibly*.

questions.q: The coffee is *___* hot to drink.
questions.explain: *too + adjective + to-infinitive* means it is more than is acceptable, so you can't do it.

questions.q: Your phone is the same *___* mine.
questions.explain: The fixed pattern is *the same as*.

questions.q: *___* it was raining, we went for a walk.
questions.explain: *even though* introduces a real fact you contrast with; *even* alone is not a conjunction.

questions.q: I could *___* hear him because of the noise.
questions.explain: *hardly* means *almost not* and is already negative, so no extra *not*.

questions.q: Which reply means *I'm sorry, the answer is no*?
questions.explain: *I'm afraid not* politely gives a negative answer; *I'm afraid so* confirms bad news.

questions.q: Could you speak more *___*, please?
questions.explain: Adverbs ending in *-ly* form comparatives with *more*: *more slowly*.

questions.q: She is *___* to win the race; she's the fastest runner.
questions.explain: *be likely to + infinitive* is the normal British pattern; *probably* would need *She will probably win*.
